facts.claim: A Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, because local authorities may ask you to prove you are not already married. DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices across Australia, through Australian embassies, high commissions and consulates overseas, and by mail.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: For Germany this general DFAT statement is overridden by the Australian Embassy Berlin: the Embassy and Consulate-General Frankfurt stopped issuing CNIs for Germany from 1 December 2021, and German authorities have been told so (F-116). Do not tell readers to get a DFAT CNI for Germany; describe the Embassy's position and the state single status route instead.

facts.claim: At least one person applying for the CNI must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident. Supporting documents: Australian citizen, a valid Australian passport; permanent resident, a valid foreign passport with evidence of permanent residence; foreign citizen partner, a valid foreign passport or photo ID; divorced, a Divorce Certificate; widowed, the deceased partner's Death Certificate. Originals or certified true copies; non-English documents need a professional English translation.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Background only for Germany (see F-100 note).

facts.claim: How to apply for a CNI through DFAT: complete the CNI application form, signing it only in front of an authorised witness (in Australia a Justice of the Peace, or an Australian Passports official at your appointment; overseas a consular official). If the overseas authority wants documents legalised, also complete a Document Legalisation Request Form. Submit by mail or in person and pay on submission. Incomplete applications are not processed. DFAT advises checking whether the CNI must be issued in the country of marriage, in which case the Australian embassy there can issue it.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage
facts.use_note: Confidence lowered for this article: conflicts with the Australian Embassy Berlin, which says it no longer issues CNIs for Germany (F-116). Prefer the Embassy's Germany-specific statement; do not say 'the Australian embassy in Germany can issue it'.

facts.claim: DFAT notarial fees from 1 January 2026, in Australian dollars: Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage AUD 181; document legalisation by Apostille AUD 105. Fees rise with CPI on 1 January each year.
facts.use_note: For Germany use only the apostille fee: 'from AUD 105 per apostille (2026 fee)', which matches the Berlin fee table (F-118). The CNI fee 'from AUD 181 (2026 fee)' is not relevant because the Embassy does not issue CNIs for Germany; mention it only if the article explains that a DFAT CNI is not the German route. Re-check after 1 January 2027.

facts.claim: DFAT does not publish a fixed processing time for legalisation: 'Processing times vary', with delays at the end of the school year and during peak holiday periods, when a request is incomplete or unpaid, or when DFAT must contact the document's issuing authority.
facts.publisher: Smartraveller (DFAT), How to get your documents legalised
facts.use_note: Matters for Germany because the birth certificate must be no older than 6 months (F-116): order it, apostille it and translate it within that window.

facts.claim: You cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law had it occurred in Australia. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where either person was already married, not old enough, too closely related, or forced to marry. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but may not be usable as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory BDM registry. Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm an overseas certificate is valid in Australia.

The Attorney-General's Department says overseas marriages cannot be performed by an Australian-authorised marriage celebrant or registered in Australia, and an overseas marriage is generally recognised in Australia if it was valid in the overseas country and would have been valid here. Some states and territories do not accept overseas marriage certificates for a change of name. Legal basis: Marriage Act 1961, Part VA (recognition of foreign marriages).
facts.use_note: Cite Part VA by name only; section text not read.

facts.claim: Passport name change after marriage: for a new passport you must link the new name to your Australian birth or citizenship certificate with an Australian RBDM marriage certificate, registered relationship certificate, or RBDM name change certificate. The Passport Office always requires an RBDM name change certificate if you were born in Australia and married overseas. Foreign certificates are accepted only if you cannot get an Australian equivalent, must be legalised, and non-English documents must be translated in full by an approved translation service.
facts.publisher: Australian Passport Office, Change of name or gender
facts.use_note: An Australian-born spouse married in Germany first registers a change of name with their state BDM before a passport in the new name. Language and format of a German marriage certificate (and any multilingual extract) not checked (N-101).

facts.claim: NSW Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages: a person legally married in Australia can take their spouse's family name without registering a change of name (the exemption is worded for marriages in Australia). Foreign documents not in English must be translated in full and stamped by a NAATI-accredited translator, with copies of the original and the translation.
facts.publisher: NSW Government, Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages
facts.use_note: NSW only; other states not checked. A German-language certificate would need a NAATI translation for NSW BDM use.

facts.claim: If you change your family name because of marriage, you can choose to get a new passport or keep using your current one, and the Australian Passport Office recommends booking travel in the name that is in your passport.
facts.use_note: Book the honeymoon in the name on the passport you will carry.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's essentials checklist says to confirm your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond the end of your trip; some countries and some airlines apply a six-month validity rule, it can apply when transiting, and getting it wrong can mean being stranded.
facts.use_note: The Germany page gives only the generic 'many countries' note (F-121). Safe wording: 'check your passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond your trip'.

facts.claim: Allow at least 6 weeks to get a passport; where possible, don't book flights without a valid passport; faster processing may be available for urgent travel at an extra fee.

Legal at home, celebration abroad: Australia has no marriage licence; the formal step is giving a Notice of Intended Marriage (NOIM) to an authorised celebrant at least 1 month and no more than 18 months before the wedding. You do not have to be an Australian citizen or permanent resident to marry in Australia. Since 12 June 2024 the NOIM can be witnessed remotely by audio-visual link, and a couple outside Australia can complete it with an authorised witness overseas (such as an Australian consular officer or a notary public, not a celebrant).
facts.reused_from: getting-married-in-jamaica B F-112 (getting-married-in-france B F-112, originally marriage-licence-requirements A F-001 to F-005)
facts.use_note: Couples living in Germany can have the NOIM witnessed at the Australian Embassy Berlin or Consulate-General Frankfurt, fee per signature (F-117, F-118).

facts.claim: Since 12 June 2024 the authorised celebrant must meet separately and in person with each party before the marriage, and must be physically present to solemnise it, together with the couple and 2 witnesses over 18. There are no video-link weddings.
facts.use_note: The Australian legal ceremony cannot be done from Germany by video.

facts.claim: After an Australian ceremony the celebrant must submit the NOIM, the Declaration of No Legal Impediment and the Official Certificate of Marriage to the BDM registry in the state or territory where the marriage took place within 14 days.
facts.publisher: Attorney-General's Department, Notice of Intended Marriage form
facts.use_note: Benefit of the home route: an Australian BDM certificate, which the Passport Office accepts directly (F-107).

facts.claim: HCCH status table for the 1961 Apostille Convention (last update 30 June 2026): Germany signed on 5 October 1961, ratified on 15 December 1965, and the Convention entered into force for Germany on 13 February 1966 (type R, ratification; declarations and notifications D,N). Australia acceded on 11 July 1994 with entry into force on 16 March 1995. Both are Contracting Parties, so an Australian public document for use in Germany is legalised by apostille rather than consular legalisation.
facts.publisher: Hague Conference on Private International Law (HCCH), Apostille Convention status table
facts.use_note: The Embassy's marriage page calls it 'The 1969 Hague Convention'; HCCH gives the Convention of 5 October 1961. Use 1961. Germany's declarations (D,N) were not opened; they do not change that apostilles apply between Australia and Germany. Which documents the Standesamt wants apostilled is confirmed with the Standesamt (batch A).

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Berlin, Marriage in Germany: Australians marrying in Germany are asked to contact the Standesamt (registry office) where they plan to marry. Requirements may vary because of regional interpretations by German courts, and the Embassy and Consulate-General Frankfurt cannot advise what you need. As a guideline the Standesamt may ask for: (1) an original birth certificate no older than 6 months, with a certified German translation if not in German and possibly an apostille; (2) for residents of Germany, no CNI: from 1 December 2021 the Embassy and Consulate-General no longer issue CNIs and German authorities have been advised you should not be required to provide one; for Australians living in Australia, an original state single status declaration (Ledigkeitsbescheinigung) from their Registry of Births, Deaths and Marriages, plus a certified translation; (3) proof of residence (Meldebescheinigung), or for Australians living in Australia, whatever the registry office accepts instead; (4) a salary or bank statement, because the marriage administration fee depends on the couple's financial status; (5) a divorce certificate or former partner's death certificate if previously married, originals and translated if applicable.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Germany (DFAT), Marriage in Germany
facts.use_note: Core Australian-side fact for this article. Present the list as the Embassy's guideline, not a complete legal list; the Standesamt decides (batch A). The page is undated and sits under the German-language section path but is in English. Do not quote fees for the Standesamt from here; none are given.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Berlin notarial services: all notarial services except apostilles are offered in person and by appointment only at the Embassy in Berlin and the Consulate-General in Frankfurt (no other locations in Germany). Services: apostilles and authentications of Australian original public documents, certified copies, proof of life, oaths and affirmations, and witnessing signatures, including on a Notice of Intended Marriage (fee per signature witnessed, so two people signing is two fees). FAQ: the Embassy and Consulate-General ceased issuing CNIs for Germany in 2021; if your Standesamt still asks for a CNI, email the Embassy and it can provide a written statement to forward to the Standesamt. The Embassy does not provide translations (it points to BDUe, bdue.de, and NAATI, naati.com.au). Often a German notary public with an English stamp plus a German apostille is enough, and notaries can be found at notar.de. Notarial fees are non-refundable.
facts.use_note: Useful 'what if the Standesamt asks for a CNI' line: ask the Embassy for its written statement. Appointment booking is via the Embassy's booking page; do not name the booking platform as a brand.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Germany passport and notarial fee table, November 2026 (exchange rate 1 AUD = 0.6284 EUR): witnessing a signature AUD 90 / EUR 57 per signature; apostille AUD 105 / EUR 66; authentication AUD 105 / EUR 66; certified copies AUD 90 / EUR 57 per copy; postage AUD 10 / EUR 6. Adult passport (10 years) AUD 611 / EUR 384. Fees are charged per document certified and per signature witnessed, and notarial fees rise on 1 January each year. Express passport processing is not available outside Australia.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Germany (DFAT), Pass- und Notargebuehren (fees)
facts.use_note: German-language fee page (the English notarial page links to an English fees page that was not fetched; figures here are the same AUD values as DFAT, F-103). Write 'from AUD 105 (about EUR 66) per apostille' and 'from AUD 90 (about EUR 57) per signature witnessed, for example on a NOIM'. EUR amounts move with the monthly exchange rate. source_date is the month shown on the table.

facts.claim: Smartraveller's overall advice for Germany is 'Exercise normal safety precautions' (still current at 17 November 2026; updated 30 October 2026). Smartraveller notes ongoing strikes, protests and demonstrations that may disrupt travel, and an ongoing terrorism threat assessed by German authorities as high, with possible targets including transport hubs, festivals and Christmas markets. Nationwide and local strikes can affect trains and airline traffic. During Oktoberfest and other major events, demand for accommodation and transport rises; expect delays.
facts.use_note: Level 1 of 4. State it plainly and link the page. Oktoberfest and Christmas markets matter for wedding-date and guest-accommodation planning; build buffers for rail strikes. Advice levels can change.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Germany entry: Germany is part of the Schengen area. Australians can travel to the Schengen area for short trips without a visa for up to 90 days in any 180-day period, and must keep their total Schengen stay within this limit. Under the EU Entry/Exit System (EES), which has started, a short stay (90 days or less) on an Australian passport means having fingerprints and photo taken and answering Schengen Border Code questions on arrival; it is free, needs no action before arrival, and may cause extended border delays. ETIAS is separate: there is no confirmed implementation date, applications are not yet open, and once it starts visa-free visitors to the 30 participating countries will need an ETIAS authorisation before travel. Dual citizens of a participating country will have to enter on that country's passport, not their Australian one. Smartraveller also points to the German Embassy Canberra for visas and the German-Australian visa exemption agreement.
facts.use_note: A wedding trip counts as a short visit; do not present 'wedding' as a named visa-free category. 90 days is shared across the whole Schengen area, so a German wedding plus a European honeymoon uses one allowance. Warn readers about fraudulent EES and ETIAS sites. The bilateral visa exemption agreement was not read (australien.diplo.de not on the approved list; N-104). Smartraveller says Germany recognises dual nationality, relevant for German-Australian couples.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Germany passport and border notes: many countries require your passport to be valid for at least 6 months before entering or departing, including for transit; the Australian Government does not make these rules. Always carry your passport when near the border or entering or leaving Germany, even within Schengen. You don't have to carry your passport day to day, but authorities can ask to see it, and you should always carry photo ID.
facts.use_note: Passport wording is generic, not a Germany-specific six-month rule; do not state one as fact. The page also says temporary checks at all German land borders run 'until 15 September 2026' (overview) and 'until September 2026' (full advice), dates already past at the page's 30 October 2026 update; do not cite the land-border checks.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Germany health and money: there is no agreement between Australia and Germany for free healthcare, so tourists pay for all medical care; hospitals need proof of insurance or funds and practitioners ask for up-front payment; get comprehensive travel insurance. Germany's currency is the euro; travelling between Germany and non-EU countries, declare amounts over 10,000 euros or equivalent, covering all forms of currency.
facts.use_note: Contrast with Malta, which has a reciprocal health care agreement; Germany does not. Cash declaration matters only for couples carrying vendor payments in cash.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Germany weather and seasonal notes: Germany experiences severe weather and natural disasters including landslides, floods, storm surges, forest fires and avalanches. Vehicles must have winter (mud and snow) tyres when there is snow, ice or frost on the road, usually needed between October and Easter, varying by region. Tick-borne encephalitis is a risk in forests and urban parks; the overview says ticks are especially active from March to November while the full advice says May to November.
facts.use_note: Only climate-adjacent statements from an approved source; no monthly temperatures or 'best months' are sourced (DWD not read, N-102). Confidence low because the tick season is stated two ways on the same page; if used, say 'spring to autumn' or quote March to November with the conflict noted. Winter tyre note is useful for guests hiring cars for a winter wedding.

facts.claim: Smartraveller Germany consular contacts: Australian Embassy, Wallstrasse 76-79, 10179 Berlin, phone +49 30 880088 0, email consular.berlin@dfat.gov.au, website germany.embassy.gov.au. Australian Consulate-General, Main Tower 28th floor, Neue Mainzer Str. 52/58, 60311 Frankfurt am Main, phone +49 69 90558 0. 24-hour Consular Emergency Centre: +61 2 6261 3305 from overseas or 1300 555 135 in Australia. Local emergency numbers: 112 for fire, rescue and medical, 110 for police.
facts.use_note: Embassy email is a generic consular mailbox and fine to publish; prefer linking the Smartraveller page. Check the Embassy site for opening hours.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Berlin, Marriage in Germany: a couple may hold the civil ceremony in their hometown or elsewhere in Germany, but an alternative location attracts higher registration fees and a longer processing period. The Notice of Intended Marriage must first be lodged at the couple's local Standesamt; once satisfied, the local Registrar transfers the case to the Standesamt of the couple's choice, which processes it again under regional requirements, and this attracts double the processing fees. If a court doubts the authenticity of Australian documents it may request an apostille, available from DFAT in Australia or from the Embassy Berlin or Consulate-General Frankfurt.
facts.publisher: Australian Embassy Germany (DFAT), Marriage in Germany
facts.use_note: Medium: the Embassy describes German process it says it cannot advise on, and the 'local Standesamt' step is written for residents of Germany; how non-resident Australians lodge notice (which Standesamt is responsible) must come from a German source (batch A, N-100). Useful to warn that a destination Standesamt outside your home district costs more and takes longer. No euro amounts given.

legal.summary: Australians marry in Germany through the Standesamt, which sets the document list (birth certificate under 6 months old with certified German translation; single status declaration from the state BDM for Australians living in Australia; proof of income; divorce or death certificate if relevant). The Australian Embassy Berlin stopped issuing CNIs from 1 December 2021. Confirm the current process with the Standesamt where you will marry and the Australian Embassy Berlin (consular.berlin@dfat.gov.au).

Embassy Berlin and Consulate-General Frankfurt offer apostilles, certified copies and witnessing (including NOIM signatures) by appointment, and a written statement for a Standesamt that still asks for a CNI. Confirm with the Australian Embassy Berlin.

Both parties to the 1961 Apostille Convention (Germany since 13 February 1966, Australia since 16 March 1995): Australian documents for Germany are apostilled by DFAT or the Embassy. Which documents need one is confirmed with the Standesamt.

No Australian registration of overseas marriages; generally recognised if valid in Germany and would be valid in Australia (Marriage Act 1961, Part VA). Confirm with DFAT, a lawyer, or your state BDM registry for name change use.
Passport in married name: an Australian-born spouse married overseas needs an RBDM name change certificate. Confirm with the Australian Passport Office and the state BDM registry.
Legal at home route: NOIM to an authorised celebrant 1 to 18 months ahead; celebrant physically present. Confirm with the Attorney-General's Department guidance and your celebrant.
